analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices with manufacturers and closes the drug benefit's coverage gap.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its January 2005 referral, despite 22 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have undone several provisions of the 2003 Medicare drug law that its supporters called gifts to industry. It would let the Health and Human Services Secretary negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers (the 2003 law explicitly barred this), repeal a federal fund that subsidized private regional Medicare plans, and restructure the drug benefit so seniors no longer fell into a gap in coverage where they paid full price. It also would waive the penalty for late enrollment in the drug benefit, cut Medicare Part B premiums using savings from tighter payments to private Medicare plans, and require public disclosure of which employers receive federal subsidies for retiree drug coverage and how much.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would gain the most: government-negotiated drug prices would lower what they and their plans pay at the pharmacy, and the coverage gap — the "doughnut hole" where beneficiaries paid full drug costs — would be eliminated. Beneficiaries who enrolled late would avoid a permanent premium penalty, dual-eligible people moving from Medicaid to Medicare would get a smoother transition, and everyone on Part B would get a premium cut funded by savings from tighter payments to private Medicare Advantage plans. Taxpayers benefit alongside them, since Medicare and Medicaid pick up much of the drug bill.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' clause of the 2003 Medicare law and directs the HHS Secretary to negotiate prices with drug manufacturers, using the same bulk-purchasing leverage as other federal buyers, and to step in if private plan prices are not fair and affordable.
Eliminates the coverage gap in the Part D drug benefit by restructuring the annual out-of-pocket threshold, so beneficiaries no longer face a stretch where they pay full price for prescriptions.

Repeals the MA Regional Plan Stabilization Fund — labeled a 'slush fund' in the bill — which was taxpayer money set aside to prop up private regional Medicare plans, and requires Medicare Advantage payments to be risk-adjusted against the whole Medicare population.

Waves the Part D late-enrollment premium penalty for anyone who signs up before 2008, and reduces Part B premiums each year by an amount equal to the savings from the tighter Medicare Advantage payments.

Requires public disclosure on the CMS website of which employers receive federal retiree drug-coverage subsidies and the total payments they receive, and directs a study of how to keep employers from dropping retiree coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose revenue if Medicare began negotiating prices, ending the 2003 law's explicit ban on government negotiation. Private Medicare Advantage insurers would lose the regional stabilization fund and face payment adjustments that would trim what they receive. The premium reductions and gap coverage would come from those savings, so the cost falls on industry revenue rather than on beneficiaries or taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and Medicare Advantage insurers

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection was that government price negotiation would cut drug company revenue and could reduce investment in developing new medicines; supporters of the 2003 law's non-interference clause argued private plans negotiating on their own would hold prices down without government involvement.

Eliminating the coverage gap and waiving late-enrollment penalties would raise the federal cost of the drug benefit, and the bill does not fully specify offsetting savings beyond the Medicare Advantage payment changes; the Part B premium cut is only as large as those estimated savings.
The bill requires a study and report on incentives for employers to keep retiree drug coverage but does not itself guarantee that employers will maintain it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits for beneficiaries are concrete and large: negotiated drug prices, no doughnut hole, no late-enrollment penalty, and a Part B premium cut. The real costs fall on drug manufacturers and Medicare Advantage insurers, and the honest trade-off is the possibility that lower drug revenue means somewhat less investment in new drugs — a cost that is real but uncertain, weighed against savings that are immediate and universal for the more than 40 million people on Medicare. The bill is a direct, focused attempt to claw back provisions its sponsors considered industry favors in the 2003 Medicare law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Dayton introduced the bill on January 24, 2005, joined by 22 Democratic cosponsors including Senator Harry Reid, the Democratic leader.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the 109th Congress.
No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and Republicans held 55 of 100 Senate seats and controlled the Finance Committee during the 109th Congress.
The Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill expired in committee; the 2003 law's ban on Medicare drug-price negotiation remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: the 2003 law's ban on Medicare price negotiation, the regional plan stabilization fund, and the drug benefit's original coverage-gap structure all stayed in place because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Medicare insurers

for.name: Sen. Mark Dayton
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 24, 2005, framing Title I as 'Eliminating Special Interest Preferences' in the 2003 Medicare law.

for.name: 22 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.role: Senate Democratic cosponsors, including party leader Harry Reid

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in the Finance Committee he chaired for two years without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The industry fought government negotiation of Medicare drug prices, the centerpiece of the bill, defending the non-interference clause it won in the 2003 Medicare law.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and Republicans, holding 55 Senate seats and the Finance chairmanship, took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 2003 law's clause barring Medicare from negotiating drug prices, which was the industry's most valuable protection — Medicare is one of the world's largest drug buyers. Industry revenue on Medicare prescriptions is paid by beneficiaries and taxpayers, so the industry's gain in the 2003 law was the public's cost.

The bill repeals the federal stabilization fund that subsidized private regional plans and tightens risk adjustment on their payments, cutting federal money flowing to the industry. Those payments come from taxpayers, so the industry's interest in keeping them runs against beneficiaries' and taxpayers' interest.

Employers keep receiving federal subsidies for retirees' drug coverage, but the bill requires them to publicly disclose the subsidy amounts and the data behind them, and directs a study of incentives to keep them from dropping retiree coverage.
